title: The Iterative Improvement Process for Websites
learningObjectives: Explain the PDCA cycle and the steps of design thinking as ways of improving a website.
Describe how A/B testing compares two options using real data, and explain why improvement is repeated in cycles.
guidingQuestion: Why is improving a website a repeated loop rather than a one-time job, and how do teams decide what to change?

blocks.text: (1) (PDCA cycle)…a method that continuously advances improvement by repeating the following four steps. It is used widely in fields such as business improvement and quality management, not just websites.

rows: Set goals and create a plan for improvement
Set the goal “reduce bounce rate by 10%” and plan a redesign of the homepage
Change the design of the homepage
Measure results and evaluate the level of goal achievement
Measure the bounce rate after the change and evaluate whether the goal (10% reduction) was achieved
Based on the evaluation, consider the next improvement measures
If the effect is sufficient, continue; if not, consider next steps such as revising headings or image placement

blocks.text: The PDCA cycle as a continuous improvement loop
(2) The important point of the PDCA cycle is not to aim for completion in one round, but to gradually improve through repetition.
(1) (Design thinking)…a way of thinking that leads to discovering problems and generating solutions from the perspective of the user. It proceeds through the following five steps.

rows: Put yourself in the user's position and understand their challenges and needs
Based on the information gleaned from empathy, clarify the problem to be solved
Generate many ideas to solve the problem
Quickly create a prototype based on the ideas
Have users try the prototype and obtain feedback from them

blocks.text: (2) Based on test results, one may go back to the empathize or define stage. Improvement proceeds back and forth, not one-way.
(1) (A/B testing)…a method in which two patterns (option A and option B) are prepared, each is shown to actual users, and data is examined to determine which is more effective.
e.g., Compare option A with a red purchase button and option B with a blue purchase button to see which gets clicked more.
① Change only one element at a time (if multiple elements are changed, it is unclear which change produced the effect).
② Make decisions only after collecting a sufficient amount of data.
